title: Quantum advantage of Monte Carlo option pricing
abstract_summary: This paper evaluates the potential quantum advantage of quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC) methods for European option pricing under realistic noise, combining systematic and statistical error modeling and relating them to gate error. The authors introduce a metric for comparing quantum and classical approaches, implement and compare a Fourier-series-based function approximation to the traditional rescaling method (finding the Fourier approach superior), and conclude that very low two-qubit gate error rates (~1e-6) are likely required for practical quantum advantage, though only on the order of ~20 logical qubits may suffice.
methodology_description: The paper evaluates the feasibility and advantage of quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC) for pricing European call options under the Black–Scholes model via noisy quantum circuit simulation. The authors discretize and truncate the analytical log-normal Black–Scholes distribution to 2^n bins (truncated around the mean by a multiple w of the standard deviation), load it exactly into n qubits using an arbitrary state preparation circuit, implement a comparator (using n ancilla qubits) to identify in-the-money states, and apply the payoff via one of two function-approximation strategies: (i) a rescaling technique that uses sin^2 approximations to generate a linear mapping, and (ii) a Fourier-series-based technique that composes sin/cos components to approximate the payoff smoothly and periodically. Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) / amplitude amplification (Grover operator) is used to estimate the payoff probability; sequences of Grover powers {m_k} (exponential schedule mk = 2^(k-1) primarily) are run, each with N_shot repeated measurements. The impact of noise is modeled by depolarizing channels applied after single- and two-qubit gates (with a fixed ratio between two- and one-qubit error rates), and an effective Grover-level coherence parameter h_Θ is fitted from gate-level noisy simulations. Statistical error bounds are computed via a Fisher-information / Cramér–Rao analysis for noisy QAE, and finite-sample corrections are estimated using maximum-likelihood simulations. Systematic errors (truncation, discretization, function-approximation) are calculated and combined in quadrature with statistical error. A quantum-advantage metric Q (ratio of classical to quantum total error for fixed sample count or runtime) is defined; the authors numerically optimize algorithmic parameters (n, w, rescaling c or Fourier truncation l_max, Grover schedule length) over parameter grids to maximize Q under a chosen error threshold, and compare quantum results to classical Monte Carlo baselines computed from the analytical Black–Scholes variance.
algorithms_used: Exact arbitrary state preparation (Shende et al.)
experimental_setup: All experiments were conducted with noisy quantum-circuit simulations using the IBM Qiskit SDK. Depolarizing noise channels were applied after each one- and two-qubit gate (except RZ); one- and two-qubit depolarizing error parameters (ε1, ε2) were used with a fixed ratio ε2 / ε1 = 30. Circuits were transpiled to the native gate set {CX, X, SX, RZ} with maximum optimization. Both gate-level noisy simulations and density-matrix expectation-value simulations were used (Qiskit’s density-matrix method where possible). Simulations were limited in practice to <=13 qubits due to computational cost; an extrapolation model for effective coherence was used for larger-n reasoning. Typical experimental choices: N_shot = 100 (per Grover step) in many optimizations, exponential Grover schedule mk = 2^(k-1), varied n in grid 1..14, w in [0.5,10], c in [1e-5,100], l_max 0..59. Coupling maps considered: all-to-all and linear (impact reported negligible on fitted Grover-level noise). MCX (multi-controlled X) used with v-chain-dirty implementation leveraging comparator ancilla.
dataset_used: Synthetic data generated from the analytical Black–Scholes log-normal distribution for the underlying asset price at maturity. European call option payoffs were evaluated at T=1. Options parameters were varied across grids: S0 = K (at-the-money), r in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}, volatility ν in {0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4}. No external empirical financial dataset was used.

experiment_input.size: Distribution discretized into 2^n bins where n varied (grid 1..14; simulations up to 13 qubits), total qubits for circuit = 2n + 1 (n state, n comparator ancilla, 1 payoff).
experiment_input.preprocessing: Truncation of distribution to [E[S_T] ± w * StdDev(S_T)] with w varied; mapping of truncated continuous support into 2^n discrete bins; exact arbitrary-state preparation used to load amplitude probabilities; comparator sets ancilla if S_i > K; function approximation applied via rescaling (parameter c) or Fourier series (smooth periodic continuation with third-order polynomial join and truncation at l_max).

pipeline_steps: 1) Choose option parameters (S0=K, r, ν, T=1) and algorithm parameters (n, w, c or l_max, Grover schedule).
2) Truncate & discretize Black–Scholes log-normal distribution to range determined by w; compute bin probabilities for 2^n bins.
3) Construct exact state-preparation circuit to load distribution amplitudes into n qubits (Shende et al. method).
4) Implement comparator circuit (uses n ancilla) to flag basis states with S_i > K; prepare payoff qubit.

5) Apply payoff function approximation: either (a) rescaling using sin^2 rotations with parameter c, or (b) Fourier-series method computing cos/sin components with truncation at l_max and smooth periodic continuation of linear segment.

6) For each Grover power m_k in schedule {m_k}, assemble Grover operator (A, A† and diffusion), run circuit N_shot times per m_k with depolarizing noise applied after gates, and measure payoff qubit probabilities.

7) Estimate amplitude/θ from measured probabilities using maximum-likelihood (simulated) or phase estimation style inference; calculate statistical error bounds via Cramér–Rao Fisher-information for noisy QAE and correct for finite-sample via empirical ML simulations.
8) Compute systematic errors separately (truncation, discretization, function approximation) and combine in quadrature with statistical errors to obtain total quantum error.
9) Compute classical Monte Carlo baseline error from analytical Black–Scholes variance for the same sample count or runtime.

10) Define and compute quantum-advantage metric Q = (classical_total_error) / (quantum_total_error); perform numerical optimization across parameter grids to maximize Q subject to an absolute error threshold (e.g., θ_thr = 1%).
11) Fit an effective Grover-level coherence parameter h_Θ from gate-level noisy simulation outputs; use extrapolation model for larger n where direct simulation infeasible.

key_findings: [supported] A Fourier series based function-approximation technique yields smaller errors and outperforms the traditional rescaling approach for function application in QAMC option pricing (shown by numerical simulations).

[supported] Systematic errors in QAMC implementations show high variability and can unpredictably dominate, making consistent quantum advantage difficult on current noisy hardware (observed in simulations).

[supported] Numerical optimization and noisy simulations indicate that two-qubit (CX) gate error rates need to be on the order of 10^-6 (or lower) for the quantum Monte Carlo method to outperform classical Monte Carlo on European option pricing.
[supported] Simulations suggest a relatively small number of logical qubits (on the order of ~20) may be sufficient to see quantum advantage, assuming very low noise / error-corrected regimes.
[supported] The optimal number of state-preparation qubits increases as hardware noise decreases; typical optimal n in the advantageous regime was found to be about 5–10 in the studied cases.

[supported] The authors introduce and use a combined metric Q (ratio of classical to quantum total error at fixed sample count or runtime) to assess quantum advantage and optimize algorithmic parameters under systematic/statistical error trade-offs.
[supported] For the set of option parameters tested, the Fourier technique outperformed the rescaling technique across a wide range of CX error rates in the simulations.

[supported] The simulations report that the ratio of systematic to statistical error at the found optima is ~0.7 for the rescaling technique and roughly an order of magnitude lower for the Fourier technique.
[supported] Current reported CX error rates on IBM devices (~10^-2 to 10^-3) are far above the paper's identified threshold for QAMC advantage.

results_summary: This paper numerically studies quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC) for European call option pricing including both statistical and multiple sources of systematic error, and explicit noisy-gate modeling (depolarizing noise). The authors introduce a joint metric Q to compare quantum vs classical total errors, optimize circuit and algorithm parameters (number of qubits, truncation, rescaling or Fourier coefficients, amplitude-estimation schedule), and compare two function-application strategies. Their simulations show the Fourier-based function approximation consistently outperforms a rescaling-based method, systematic errors are significant and erratic, and that achieving a practical quantum advantage would require two-qubit gate error rates far below present hardware (CX ~10^-6 or lower). They also find that a relatively small logical qubit count (order 20) could suffice if noise is reduced sufficiently, but current devices (CX ~10^-2–10^-3) are inadequate.
performance_claims: Two-qubit (CX) gate error rate must be ≲ 10^-6 (paper's estimated threshold) for the quantum method to outperform classical Monte Carlo in their European option pricing benchmarks.
A low number of logical qubits—around 20—may be sufficient to achieve quantum advantage under sufficiently low noise.
Typical optimal number of state-preparation qubits in the advantageous regime: 5–10.
Ratio of systematic to statistical error at optimized points: ~0.7 for rescaling technique; ~0.07 (order of magnitude lower) for the Fourier technique (averaged over tested options).
Sample sizes used in optimization examples: N_shot ~100 per Grover step in many of the optimizations (small-sample regime emphasized).
QAE retains idealized quadratic error scaling O(1/N) in the noiseless theory and is used as the basis for quantum speedup analysis.
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors do not demonstrate empirical quantum advantage on real hardware; rather, they present noisy numerical simulations and optimization that indicate quantum advantage could be possible only under very low two-qubit error rates (~10^-6) and modest qubit counts (~20). Thus the advantage is conditional on technological improvements (likely error correction) and remains speculative based on current hardware.
limitations: Systematic errors show high variability and unpredictable behavior, which greatly affects feasibility on noisy quantum hardware (author-stated).
Quantum advantage requires extremely low two-qubit (CX) gate error rates (around 10^-6), far below current hardware error rates (author-stated).
State preparation is costly: loading arbitrary probability distributions exactly requires circuits whose cost grows exponentially with qubit number (author-stated).
The study assumes the probability distribution is known and does not include the cost or errors of generating the distribution on the quantum device (author-stated).
Function application is approximate (rescaling or truncated Fourier methods) and introduces systematic error; Fourier requires truncation (lmax) which is a source of systematic error (author-stated).

Noise is modeled using a simplified depolarizing channel and an effective coherence parameter for the Grover operator; this is a simplification and may not capture all real-device noise characteristics (author-stated).
Simulations were limited to at most 13 qubits due to computational cost; results for larger qubit counts rely on an extrapolation formula (26) rather than direct simulation (author-stated).

The work used the standard (non-adaptive) QAE / Grover operator only; potential improvements from adaptive measurements, quantum Fisher information bounds, or modified Grover variants were not investigated (author-stated).
Assumption that the classical Monte Carlo baseline is free of systematic errors (author-stated).
Depolarizing noise was applied after every gate except RZ and a fixed gate error ratio (ò2/ò1 = 30) was used; hardware-specific error asymmetries and crosstalk were not modelled (author-stated).

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) / amplitude amplification can in principle reduce Monte Carlo sampling error for European option pricing, and the paper defines a quantitative metric Q comparing classical and quantum total error.

#idea:quantum-advantage — A Fourier-series-based function-approximation for the payoff mapping outperforms the traditional rescaling (sin^2) method in terms of systematic error for the tested option setups.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Under realistic depolarizing noise models and fitted Grover-level coherence, practical quantum advantage requires extremely low two-qubit gate error rates (on the order of 1e-6), implying that near-term NISQ devices are unlikely to achieve advantage for this task.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Only modest logical-qubit counts (~20 logical qubits) may be sufficient in principle, but stringent gate-fidelity requirements and error accumulation remain the limiting factors.

#idea:quantum-advantage — The authors combine systematic (truncation, discretization, function-approximation) and statistical errors via Fisher-information / Cramér–Rao analysis and finite-sample ML corrections to obtain realistic total-error comparisons against classical MC baselines.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Numerical optimization over discretization (n), truncation width (w), function-approximation parameters, and Grover schedules is used to maximize the advantage metric Q under error constraints.
contradictions: contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — The paper finds that, contrary to optimistic claims of near-term quantum speedup for Monte Carlo option pricing, achieving a net advantage over classical Monte Carlo requires two-qubit gate error rates around 1e-6, which are far below current hardware — i.e., quantum advantage is not imminent under realistic noise.

contradiction:scalability — Although the authors extrapolate that ~20 logical qubits could suffice, their gate-level noisy simulations are limited to ≤13 qubits and require an extrapolated effective-coherence model for larger n; this contradicts any claims that current simulation evidence directly demonstrates scalability to practically sized problems without speculative extrapolation.
